chunk_findings.detail: `depth` computes the number of ancestors between an item and its phase/root, then unconditionally truncates the result to 6. Depth is a property of well-formed input, not only of the malformed cycles the comment cites: for a phase `P` with a legitimate chain `P → t1 → t2 → t3 → t4 → t5 → t6 → t7` (each task's `parent` being the previous one), `closure`/`above` yields 7 ancestors, but `depth` returns `min(7, 6) == 6`. `board_rows` feeds that value straight into the markdown indentation and into the `"depth"` field of `board --json` (via `rows(...)`), so a task nested more than six levels below its phase is rendered at the wrong indent level (and reports the wrong depth in JSON). The whole point of this change is that the board must stay byte-identical while the tallies are recomputed in core; this new, silent cap changes the board for any hierarchy deeper than six, and the `min(..., 6)` is not what protects against cycles anyway — a parent cycle is handled by `closure`'s own visited-set (the `last.parent == last.id` term only reacts to a cycle that has already terminated), so the bound only ever bites legitimate deep nesting.

chunk_findings.detail:
`progress.tally` is documented by the inline comment as counting at *every depth* ("the one phase rule: every depth, abandoned out"), i.e. it descends into sub-tasks of the tasks it is handed. The old code counted exactly the elements of `q.tasks_under(p.id)` (minus abandoned) and compared `n_done == len(tasks)`, and the `tasks`/`rows` list used for rendering is still taken directly from `under`. So when a phase has a nested sub-task, `n.live` and `n.done` no longer equal `len(tasks)` / `n_done`.

Concrete failure: a phase marked `DONE` whose direct tasks are all `DONE` but which has one nested sub-task still `RUNNING`. Old: `n_done == len(tasks)` is true, so the phase hits the `done += 1; continue` short-circuit and produces only a phase count. New: `n.done != n.live`, so the branch is skipped and a phase card is emitted, with `done`/`total` that include the nested task that never appears in `tasks`/`rows`. This changes `board --json`/markdown output for any hierarchy with nested sub-tasks, contradicting the stated invariant that those outputs must be byte-identical (this change is not in the list of the three permitted visible changes). The same divergence applies to `"done": n.done, "total": n.live` on non-done phases, where the card total can now exceed the number of rendered rows.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor drops the explicit non-empty guard that the old expression carried. Previously the test was `c := _phase_counts(items, p.id))[1] and c[0] == c[1]`, i.e. a phase was only "ready to close" if it had at least one live task child (`total != 0`) *and* all of them were done. The replacement is just `... and PR.phase_tally(st, p.id).complete`, and per the comment on the line above, `phase_tally` deliberately excludes abandoned tasks from the total. For a phase that is not DONE but has zero non-abandoned tasks — a freshly created phase, or a phase whose tasks were all marked ABANDONED — `phase_tally` yields `done == 0`, `live == 0`, so a `complete` predicate of the natural shape `done == live` evaluates to True. The progress line then appends `, N ready to close` for a phase that has nothing left to close, whereas the old code suppressed it (the `c[1]` term was falsy). This is a fourth visible change, not one of the three intended ones (B01281f654e/Bb24939611d/B45b55be6a4), so the progress line is no longer byte-identical to before for any state containing an empty or fully-abandoned phase. The every-depth counting intended by Bb24939611d is achieved by `phase_tally`'s recursion; the non-empty guard it replaced needs to be preserved (or `Tally.complete` must be defined as `live > 0 and done == live`) to avoid the spurious "ready to close".

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own rule block states that a phase's tasks are its *live* tasks and that "an abandoned task is SETTLED, not outstanding", so a phase cannot close only "while any of them is open". With `complete = self.live > 0 and self.done == self.live`, a phase whose every task is abandoned yields `Tally(done=0, live=0, abandoned=N)` and therefore `complete is False` — even though no live task is open, exactly the situation the rule says is settled. Concretely, `tally([t_state == ABANDONED])` returns `Tally(0, 0, 1)` and `Tally(0, 0, 1).complete` is `False`, so any consumer using `complete` to render a phase as done/ready-to-close (phase list / progress line) will keep such a phase open forever. The `live > 0` guard conflates "no live work left" with "never had any work"; dropping the guard (testing `done == live` directly) would make an all-abandoned phase settle as the rule describes.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old expression pinned the emitted order to `_ORDER = (DONE, RUNNING, REVIEW, OPEN, BLOCKED, ABANDONED)`:
`[{"state": s, "n": counts[s]} for s in _ORDER if counts[s]]`. The new one iterates `counts.items()`, i.e. whatever order `progress.state_counts()` happens to produce. Nothing in the diff guarantees that order. A natural implementation (`{}` built in first-encountered order, or `collections.Counter`) emits states in task-encounter order, not the canonical `_ORDER`. Concrete case: a project whose only two tasks appear in the store as RUNNING then DONE yields `task_counts == [{"state": RUNNING, ...}, {"state": DONE, ...}]`, whereas before it was `[{"state": DONE, ...}, {"state": RUNNING, ...}]`. `status --json` is then no longer byte-identical to the golden, and this is not one of the three allowed visible changes (phase list, progress sub-task depth, progress phase name).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_status.py:_data (`task_counts`)

chunk_findings.detail: `counts[DONE]` used to be unconditionally safe: `counts = {s: sum(...) for s in _ORDER}` always created a `DONE` key. The replacement `progress.state_counts(tasks)` has no such contract stated anywhere; if it returns only the states that actually occur (the obvious `Counter(t.state for t in tasks)` shape), then any project with zero completed tasks makes `counts[DONE]` raise `KeyError`, crashing the `status` export. Input that demonstrates it: `tasks` containing only RUNNING/OPEN tasks (or an empty project) -> `state_counts` has no `DONE` entry -> `KeyError: DONE` on this line. Note the retained `if n` filter on `task_counts` is exactly the "drop zero counts" behaviour that suggests zero entries are otherwise present, but the subscript on the very next statements assumes they are present for `DONE` — the two assumptions conflict unless `state_counts` materialises every state.

The run records it parses are written by `schedule.py`, which now stamps them with `clock.now_utc()` — a UTC instant — so their naive wall-clock text is UTC, and reading it back as *local* shifts every timestamp by the host's UTC offset. Concrete case: a run at 12:00 UTC stored as `...T12:00:00`, read on a UTC−05:00 host, becomes epoch for 17:00Z, i.e. `last` is 5 h too large; then `age_days = (now - last)/86400` is 5 h too small, so a cadence sitting on its period boundary is reported as *not* due, and for the due ones `since` renders a smaller `clock.fmt_age(now - last, "days", places=1)` value (e.g. "6.8 days" instead of "7.0 days"). Both the due/not-due decision and the rendered `since` string therefore differ from the pre-refactor output on any non-UTC host — the byte-identical guarantee fails, and no test in the formatting suite covers it.

chunk_findings.detail: The original expression floored whole minutes: `f"{w['waiting_s'] // 60}m so far"`. The new call passes only the seconds and relies on `clock.fmt_age`'s default formatting. chunk_findings.detail: The refactor does not just rename the helper: `epoch(r["at"])` (no keyword) became `clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local")`, which hard-codes how offset-less timestamps are decoded. The run timestamps in `runs` are written by the same clock helpers that write UTC (cf. `at = given or clock.now_utc()` in `schedule.py`, and the `%H:%M:%SZ` UTC rendering), so any log entry serialized without a `+00:00` offset — which the intent says must keep producing byte-identical output — is now interpreted in the process's local timezone rather than whatever the old `progress.epoch` default did. Concretely, with `TZ=America/New_York` and a run stored as `"2024-01-01T10:00:00"` (10:00 UTC), the decoded `last` moves by +5h (05:00 UTC), so `age_days = (now - last)/86400` is off by ~0.21 days; for a daily cadence near the `age_days >= days` boundary this flips the `due` verdict and also changes the `"since"` string emitted via `clock.fmt_age(now - last, "days", places=1)`. The format-pinning test `tests/test_clock_format.py` only pins rendering, not this decoding, so it would not catch the shift. The change is output-preserving only if the removed `progress.epoch` already defaulted to local; if its default was UTC (consistent with the rest of the module writing UTC), this is a regression.

chunk_findings.detail: The old code inserted `lease.ttl_s // 60` directly into the f-string (`past its {lease.ttl_s // 60} min TTL`). For an `int` TTL this is an `int`, and the new code matches. But `clock.fmt_age` wraps the quotient in `int(...)`, whereas the old TTL expression had no `int()`. So for a non-integer `ttl_s` (e.g. a TTL read from config/JSON as a float), the rendered text changes: with `lease.ttl_s = 90.0`, the old line rendered `past its 1.0 min TTL` (`90.0 // 60 == 1.0`, formatted by the f-string), while the new one renders `past its 1 min TTL` (`int(90.0 // 60) == 1`). The `idle` and `ago` values are unaffected because their original expressions already applied `int(...)` (`int((now - lease.renewed_at) // 60)` and `max(0, int(... // 60))`), so only this third, newly-`int()`-wrapped TTL value is a behavior change. chunk_findings.detail: The old `_now()` was a function defined in `rules.py` whose body called `datetime.now(UTC)` at *call* time. The replacement `_now = clock.now_utc` is a module-level **alias** that captures whatever function object `clock.now_utc` was at import time, so it no longer follows the `clock` module. Concretely: in an environment where time is frozen by replacing the clock (e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.core.clock, "now_utc", lambda: FIXED)` — or any production wiring that swaps the clock), `gates/runner.py`'s `compact_at` is re-imported and re-resolved per call and will stamp the frozen time into log filenames, while `rules._now()` keeps returning the real wall clock and writes real timestamps into the rule data, so two "now" writers in the same process disagree. This is also inconsistent with the way the other three sites invoke their helper (`clock.fmt_minute(...)`, `clock.iso_at(...)`, `compact_at()`) rather than pre-binding it. The fix is to keep a thin call-through (`def _now(): return clock.now_utc()`) or to call `clock.now_utc()` directly wherever `_now` is used.

chunk_findings.detail: The old expression was `f"... {w['waiting_s'] // 60}m so far"`, i.e. floor division that always yields whole minutes. It has been replaced with `clock.fmt_age(w['waiting_s'])`, dropping the explicit floor. For the two call sites that pass an explicit `places=1` the replacement is the same arithmetic (`secs / 60` formatted to 1 decimal), which shows `fmt_age` takes raw seconds and renders `seconds / 60` with `places` decimals. With the default `places=0` that is `f"{secs/60:.0f}m"`, which *rounds* rather than truncates. Given `waiting_s = 90` the old line printed `... 1m so far`, the new one prints `... 2m so far` (1.5 rounds to 2); given `waiting_s = 3599` the old line printed `59m`, the new one prints `60m` (59.983 → 60). chunk_findings.detail: In the success branch, `_decode(out, "replace" if raw else errors).strip()` and the same for `stderr` decode git's raw output with `errors="strict"` whenever the caller did not pass `z=True`/`binary=True` and did not override `errors`. Callers that parse or compare output get different results purely because the command was killed at its bound. The fix is to pin `encoding="utf-8"` for the subprocess call (so both paths agree) or to decode the timeout bytes with the same encoding the wrapper used for the completed case.

The new code inspects `p.err` instead, but `p.err` is also the field used one branch earlier as the text for `"could not execute: {p.err}"` — i.e. it is the execution/spawn-error field, set when the process never started. Those two uses are mutually exclusive: a process that starts and exits 127 never fails to spawn, so `p.err` is empty (or `None`) in exactly the case this branch is trying to detect, while the shell's "sh: line 1: foo: command not found" text is part of the merged `p.output` that was just assigned to `out`. The concrete failure is a compound gate command such as `gdef.command = "nope | tee log"` (pre-flight cannot inspect pipes): the shell runs, writes the not-found diagnostic to stderr, exits 127, `p.code in (126, 127)` is true, but `_looks_like_not_found(p.err)` is false because `p.err` holds nothing, so the gate is reported as an ordinary failed command with `"exit": 127` instead of `"unavailable"`, changing the retry/abort decision. In the variant where `err` is `None`, `p.err.strip()[:200]` in the same branch raises `AttributeError` and takes down the gate runner, whereas `subprocess` gave `""` and the old code guarded with `(p.stderr or "")`. Either the diagnostic must come from `p.output` (the merged child output) or `p.err` must not be reused as the spawn-error text.

chunk_findings.detail: The `try` in `run_shell` wraps the entire `_shell_group(...)` call, and `_shell_group` invokes the caller-supplied `on_tick` callback repeatedly on this thread while the command runs. Any `ValueError` or `OSError` raised *by that callback* is therefore caught and converted into `ShellResult(None, err=str(exc), could_not_run=True)` — i.e. the result claims the command never started, even though it did start and may still be running. This is a plausible real path: `on_tick` is used to renew a lease during long gates, and a lease renewal that fails with a network error raises an `OSError`/`ConnectionError` (a subclass of `OSError`). Given that input, `run_shell` returns `could_not_run=True` and the caller silently treats a live command / transient network failure as "the command could not be run" (the exact meaning the `ShellResult` docstring attaches to a missing tool or refused environment), instead of surfacing the callback's bug. It also contradicts `run_shell`'s own docstring, which insists that caller bugs around `on_tick` "still raise ValueError". The exception scope should be narrowed to the command's own launch failure (e.g. catch only around `Popen`/spawn), or `on_tick` failures should be allowed to propagate.

chunk_findings.detail: The old code built the recorded output from both streams: `out = (p.stdout or "") + (p.stderr or "")`. The new code sets `out = p.output`, and the result object exposes stderr separately as `p.err` (that is exactly the field used just below for not-found detection and for the `could_not_run` message). With `output` meaning the process' stdout, any gate whose diagnostics are written to stderr silently disappears from the recorded result: the subsequent `"output_digest": digest(out)` and `"output_bytes": len(out)` now reflect stdout only. Concrete case: a gate command `sh -c 'echo "warning: X" 1>&2; exit 0'` produced `out == "warning: X\n"` before (digest non-empty, `output_bytes > 0`) and now produces `out == ""` (`digest("")`, `output_bytes == 0`). Any consumer that compares `output_digest` to detect whether a gate's output changed, or that reports `output_bytes`, will treat runs that differ only on stderr as identical. If the intent of the new API was stdout+stderr, this should be `out = p.output + (p.err or "")`; if the intent was stdout-only, the digest/bytes consumers downstream need to be made aware, because their input just changed for every stderr-emitting gate.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old body sent the signal with the child's pid *used directly as the process-group id*:
`os.killpg(thing.pid, signal.SIGKILL)`. The replaced code in `onboard_verify._stop`, by contrast, resolved the group with `os.killpg(os.getpgid(proc.pid), ...)`. Those two are not equivalent once the group leader is gone: if the shell (the session/group leader, started with `start_new_session=True`) has already exited while the reviewer it spawned is still alive, `os.getpgid(thing.pid)` raises `ProcessLookupError`, whereas `os.killpg(thing.pid, ...)` still succeeds because the group id remains valid as long as any member lives. If the shared `P.kill_group` is implemented the way the two other refactored call sites were (resolve via `os.getpgid`, fall back to `proc.kill()`), then in the scenario "reviewer shell exited (or daemonized its child), reviewer still running, `_abort(thing)` called", the `getpgid` lookup fails, the `proc.kill()` fallback is a no-op (the Popen is already reaped / the pid is gone), and the reviewer `_abort` was specifically written to kill — "the shell AND the reviewer it started" — survives. The old `os.killpg(thing.pid, ...)` form would have delivered SIGKILL to that surviving group member. The call site was changed to the shared helper without preserving the pid-as-pgid semantics it relied on.

chunk_findings.detail: The fix for the earlier tick-callback finding only guards the `except (OSError, ValueError)` branch with `if from_tick: raise`; the preceding `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:` branch does not consult `from_tick` at all. `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` is a `SubprocessError`, i.e. not an `OSError`/`ValueError`, so if the caller-supplied `on_tick` callback raises it (a very natural thing for a lease-renewal callback that shells out to a CLI or otherwise uses `subprocess.run(..., timeout=...)`), `tick()` records it in `from_tick` and re-raises, it propagates out of `_shell_group`, and `run_shell` catches it here and returns `ShellResult(None, _text(exc.output), _text(exc.stderr), timed_out=True, ...)`. The caller is then told the *operator's command* timed out and was killed, when in fact the command may still be running normally and only the callback's own subprocess timed out — the same "attribute the callback's trouble to the command" defect that finding #1 was about, just through the other handler. The `if from_tick: raise` guard needs to be present in the `TimeoutExpired` branch as well (before returning the timed-out result).

chunk_findings.detail: The old body wrapped the run in `try: ... except subprocess.TimeoutExpired ... except (OSError, ValueError) as exc: return "unavailable", {"reason": f"could not execute: {exc}", ...}`. The new body has no `except` at all: it assumes `run_shell` never raises and instead reports every failure through `p.timed_out` / `p.could_not_run`. But `run_shell` is invoked with `on_tick=on_tick` and runs that callback *on this thread* (that is the whole point of the ticking path). Prior finding #1 was confirmed precisely because a `ValueError`/`OSError` raised by `on_tick` was being swallowed into `could_not_run=False`; the fix for it stops `run_shell` from mislabeling such an error, which means the error is no longer contained inside `run_shell` either. With the gate-level handler deleted, the exception now escapes `run_command_gate` entirely. Concrete case: a long gate run with `on_tick` = lease renewal, where a transient renewal failure raises `OSError`/`ConnectionResetError` after the command has started. Under the old code the gate degraded to `("unavailable", {"reason": "could not execute: ..."})`; with this diff the exception propagates out of `run_command_gate` (there is no `p.could_not_run` flag set for it), so a lease-renewal blip aborts gate evaluation instead of yielding an `unavailable` result. The fix for finding #1 only relocates where the callback error goes; it does not answer that `run_command_gate` lost the handler that used to contain it.

The change's stated scope is that `proc.run_shell` replaces `gates._run_ticking`, `run_command_gate`, `ci`, `bisect`, `review` and the private `killpg` copies. The edit removes `ddflow.services.ci` and `ddflow.services.gates.runner` (consistent with that scope) but it *also* removes `ddflow.services.onboard_tests`, a module the change does not claim to touch, while *retaining* `ddflow.services.bisect` and `ddflow.services.review`, which the change does claim to convert. Concretely: if `ddflow.services.onboard_tests` still has its `subprocess` import (as it does not appear anywhere in the described conversion), the recorded baseline no longer contains that `module -> subprocess` pair while the actual import set still does, so the import-linter guard fails on the missing allowance; conversely, if `bisect`/`review` were fully converted, the retained entries fail it the other way. The two asymmetries (converted module kept, unconverted module dropped) cannot both be right, and the fix is to reconcile this baseline with the actual post-change set of `subprocess` importers rather than editing entries that the stated change neither adds nor removes.

chunk_findings.detail: The fix for the earlier tick-callback finding only guards the `except (OSError, ValueError)` branch with `if from_tick: raise`; the preceding `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:` branch does not consult `from_tick` at all. `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` is a `SubprocessError`, i.e. not an `OSError`/`ValueError`, so if the caller-supplied `on_tick` callback raises it (a very natural thing for a lease-renewal callback that shells out to a CLI or otherwise uses `subprocess.run(..., timeout=...)`), `tick()` records it in `from_tick` and re-raises, it propagates out of `_shell_group`, and `run_shell` catches it here and returns `ShellResult(None, _text(exc.output), _text(exc.stderr), timed_out=True, ...)`. The `if from_tick: raise` guard needs to be present in the `TimeoutExpired` branch as well (before returning the timed-out result).

chunk_findings.detail: The old body wrapped the run in `try: ... except subprocess.TimeoutExpired ... except (OSError, ValueError) as exc: return "unavailable", {"reason": f"could not execute: {exc}", ...}`. The new body has no `except` at all: it assumes `run_shell` never raises and instead reports every failure through `p.timed_out` / `p.could_not_run`. But `run_shell` is invoked with `on_tick=on_tick` and runs that callback *on this thread* (that is the whole point of the ticking path). Prior finding #1 was confirmed precisely because a `ValueError`/`OSError` raised by `on_tick` was being swallowed into `could_not_run=False`; the fix for it stops `run_shell` from mislabeling such an error, which means the error is no longer contained inside `run_shell` either. chunk_findings.detail:
The old code extracted the resolved MERGE_HEAD with `head.stdout.strip()`, but the new code passes `head.out` straight into the second git call:

```python
head = G.run(".", "rev-parse", "-q", "--verify", "MERGE_HEAD", timeout=G.PROBE_TIMEOUT)
merging = head.ok and (
    G.run(".", "merge-base", "--is-ancestor", head.out, "HEAD", timeout=G.PROBE_TIMEOUT).code
    != 0
)
```

`G.run` returns a raw `GitResult` whose `.out` is the decoded stdout/`err` text (that is why the sibling sites in this same diff still need `paths()`/slicing to post-process it, e.g. `docscheck._tree`'s `r.paths()` and `r.err[:200]`). If `.out` carries the trailing newline that `git rev-parse` emits (`"<40-hex>\n"`), then `merge-base --is-ancestor "<40-hex>\n" HEAD` is given a 41-char object name. Git cannot parse `"<sha>\n"` as a revision (it is neither a 40-char hex oid nor a valid ref name), so the command fails with a non-zero/128 exit even though MERGE_HEAD *is* an ancestor of HEAD.

Concrete failure: a stale or planted `MERGE_HEAD` that points at HEAD (the exact rubber-duck case the comment says this code was written to reject). Old behaviour: `merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD` exits 0 → `merging` is False → the trailer rule still applies. New behaviour: the trailing newline makes `merge-base` exit non-zero while `head.ok` is True, so `merging` becomes True, the ordinary commit is treated as an in-progress merge, and the trailer rule is bypassed again — reintroducing the exemption the change claims to fix. Either `head.out.strip()` is required, or the wrapper must guarantee `.out` is already trimmed (the container hunks that dropped `.strip()` only survive because `bool("x\n")` happens to still be True, so they do not demonstrate that `.out` is stripped).

chunk_findings.detail: The old call was `P.run(["git", "-C", str(repo), "ls-files", "-z", "--cached"], capture_output=True, timeout=60)`; the replacement `G.git_paths(repo, "ls-files", "--cached")` passes no timeout at all, while the two sibling conversions in the same file deliberately carry their timeouts forward (`_grep` keeps `timeout=120`, `staged_diff` keeps `timeout=120`). So this is the only one of the three sites whose run is no longer bounded. chunk_findings.detail:
The old body was `out = (r.stdout or "").strip(); return out if r.returncode == 0 and out else None`, i.e. it always handed callers a whitespace-trimmed string. The new body returns `r.out` verbatim. `infra.git.run` is the low-level argv wrapper: its `.out` is the raw captured stdout — the very value the old code had to call `.strip()` on — and every successful git command terminates stdout with a newline. So given a repo whose `git config --get remote.origin.url` prints `https://example.com/x.git
`, `_git` now returns `"https://example.com/x.git
"` instead of `"https://example.com/x.git"`. That value is fed into this module's `urlparse`/`url2pathname` path handling and into comparisons against the resolved `root`, so the parsed local path becomes `.../x.git
` and the install-kind/source classification is corrupted. The `.strip()` (or an equivalent trim) needs to be restored; the type annotation `str | None` hides the fact that the returned string is no longer normalized.

chunk_findings.detail: The `below` branch special-cases `count == 0` with `f"now delete {path} in this same change, so the sites cannot grow back."`, where `path = _module_baseline_path(kind, module).relative_to(ROOT)`. Per the stated design this baseline is "a directory with one small file per top-level package (api, services, infra, core, surfaces, views)" keyed by *full module name* (the earlier finding enumerated modules such as `ddflow.services.gates.mutation`, `ddflow.services.gates.runner`, and `ddflow.services.sessions`, all of which live in the same top-level package `services`). So `_module_baseline_path` must map several distinct modules onto one shared package file (e.g. `tests/guard_baselines/write_text/services.toml`). Concrete failure: suppose `ddflow.services.gates.mutation` goes from 2 sites to 0 while `ddflow.services.gates.runner` still has 1 site and `ddflow.services.sessions` still has 2. The guard emits, for `mutation`, "now delete tests/guard_baselines/write_text/services.toml in this same change". An author who follows that instruction deletes the file and thereby drops the `runner`/`sessions` entries; the next run then reports those modules with `baseline = 0` in `above` and the guard fails on previously-clean modules. The remediation text is wrong: for a package file shared by sibling modules it must say to remove that module's entry, not to delete the file (the old single-file guard had no delete variant at all, so this special case is newly introduced).

chunk_findings.detail:
The assertion that gives this test its name can never execute. In

```python
with s.hold(0) as slot, pytest.raises(SlotsTimeout), s.try_hold(-3):
    assert slot.index == 0
```

the body of a `with` statement runs only after *every* context manager's `__enter__` has returned. `s.try_hold(-3)` raises `SlotsTimeout` from `__enter__` (that is exactly what `pytest.raises` was put there to swallow), so control jumps to `pytest.raises.__exit__`, which returns `True`; `s.hold(0).__exit__` is then called with `(None, None, None)` and the statement completes. The body — `assert slot.index == 0` — is never reached, on any input.

Consequence: nothing in the file verifies the "clamp a sub-1 limit to 1" behaviour at all. An implementation where `Slots.hold(0)` clamps the *limit* to 1 for the blocking check but hands out an arbitrary index (say 5, or index 0 of a differently-sized pool), or where the limit is clamped to any value ≥ 1, still passes this test. The only thing the test actually pins down is that `hold(0)` does not itself raise; the claim in the test name is unasserted. The likely intended shape is

```python
with s.hold(0) as slot:
    assert slot.index == 0
    with pytest.raises(SlotsTimeout), s.try_hold(-3):
        pass
```

which puts the assertion in a body that runs.

(Everything else in the file — the fake-clock timeout assertion `ft.now >= 103`, the empty-sleep check for a zero timeout, the lowering/raising-limit cases, and the flock subprocess kill case — checks a condition that a wrong implementation would actually violate, so there is nothing to report there.)

The added/deleted detection (`new file mode` / `deleted file mode`) is only run in the `seen` branch, i.e. only when a `---`/`+++`/rename line was found. Concretely, `git diff --cached` after `touch empty && git add empty` produces:

```
diff --git a/empty b/empty
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..e69de29
```

`parse_section` returns `FileDiff(head, "empty", "empty")`, contradicting the dataclass contract "old ... None for an added file". The same happens for a file deleted to empty, and for every binary add/delete (`Binary files /dev/null and b/x differ`, no `---`/`+++`): e.g. a deleted binary gets `new == "x"` where it should be `None`. Any consumer using `f.old is None`/`f.new is None` (rather than `path`) to decide add vs delete vs rename misclassifies these files.

`FileDiff.old`/`new` are documented as "None for an added file" / "None for a deleted file", and the `seen` branch carefully computes `added`/`deleted` from the `new file mode` / `deleted file mode` lines. diff --git a/logo.png b/logo.png
```
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..1234567
Binary files /dev/null and b/logo.png differ
```

Applying the existing `added`/`deleted` scan in this branch would fix it without affecting the genuine mode-change case (`old mode`/`new mode` lines don't start with `new file mode`, so a mode-only section still yields `old == new == path`).

`header_path` unquotes and then strips `a/`/`b/`, assuming the prefix is present. `_from_header_line` explicitly accommodates `diff.noprefix` output (`if left == right: return left, left`), but the `---`/`+++` path does not, so under `diff.noprefix=true` a file whose real path begins with `b/` is corrupted. diff --git b/logo.png b/logo.png
```
index 1111111..2222222 100644
--- b/logo.png
+++ b/logo.png
@@ -1 +1 @@
-old
+new
```
`old = header_path("--- b/logo.png", "a/") = "b/logo.png"` (correct) but `new = header_path("+++ b/logo.png", "b/") = "logo.png"` (wrong), so `FileDiff` reports a spurious rename and `touched_paths` yields `{"b/logo.png", "logo.png"}`, inventing a path that does not exist (a file named `a/...` fails symmetrically). chunk_findings.detail: The fallback comparison is lossy: `os.fsencode(p).decode("utf-8", "replace")` replaces *every* invalid byte with U+FFFD, and the new comment states the diff side is decoded the same way, so any two paths that differ only in non-UTF-8 bytes collapse to the same value. Concretely, with `core.quotepath` at its default and two changed non-UTF-8 files, say `a\xe9` and `a\x80`, `git status -z` keeps them distinct (they arrive as surrogate-escaped strings, as the comment says), so `changed` holds both. If the diff silently drops `a\x80` and shows only `a\xe9`, `unidiff.touched_paths(diff)` yields `{"a\ufffd"}`. For `p = "a\x80"` the exact check `p not in shown` is true, but the fallback maps it to the identical `"a\ufffd"`, so it is judged present and the function returns `(True, [])` — the exact "silent omission" of a changed file that this guard exists to catch goes unreported. The removed `_c_quoted` matched the distinct octal spellings git actually emits (`a\200` vs `a\351`), so the default `core.quotepath=true` case was previously collision-free; this change reintroduces the collision for every repo, not just `quotepath=false` ones.
